sources.title: Candido Portinari (Q319532), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-04): English label 'Candido Portinari', description 'Brazilian painter (1903-1962)', born 1903-12-29, died 1962-02-06 (the entry also holds a year-only death value). No Korean label and no Korean Wikipedia article exist. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

'Portinari of Brazil', exhibition catalogue, The Museum of Modern Art, New York, with the Detroit Institute of Arts, 1940 (catalogue PDF read through its text layer), containing a biographical profile by Florence Horn (his schooling, years of portraits made from photographs, the Prix de Voyage trip on which he painted almost nothing, the unsold pictures of Brazilian life he kept painting, his refusal to follow hints about whom to paint, the yearly Carnival pictures, the 1935 Carnegie honorable mention, the 1938 Ministry of Education frescoes, the 269-item 1939 show with details for the frescoes) and an essay by Robert C. Smith of the Library of Congress calling him one of the most gifted living artists and describing his varied portrait, fresco, gouache and fantasy styles. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE (contemporary museum catalogue; admiring, and independent of the later Projeto Portinari material).

University of Sao Paulo, Portal Latinoamericano, biographical entry 'Portinari, Candido', read in full: born 1903 on a coffee plantation in Brodosqui, trained at the National School of Fine Arts in Rio (1919-1921), won the 1928 Foreign Travel Prize, Baile na Roca rejected by the school jury in 1924, Evicted (1934), Cafe (Carnegie honorable mention), the Ministry of Education frescoes 1935-1939, the 1939 New York World's Fair panels, MoMA and Detroit solo shows (1940), the Library of Congress mural (1942 on this page), the Pampulha church mural, Guerra e Paz at the United Nations (1956), Burial in a Hammock chosen at Brussels in 1958, and sharp criticism from advocates of abstraction in 1955. Note: the page gives the 1945 candidacy and the paint-poisoning illness, which are not used.

Projeto Portinari (the artist's archive), '10 Facts About Portinari', Google Arts & Culture story, read in full: about 5,000 artworks catalogued of which few were exhibited in his lifetime, portraits painted from enlarged photographs to fund his training, the 1928 prize trip, the 1940 MoMA solo show, the Pampulha church mural and its long refusal of consecration, and the later archive. Holder-curated and favourable.

Projeto Portinari, 'From the Coffee Plantation to the UN', Google Arts & Culture story, read in full: a dated career chronology (ENBA 1920, Paris 1929 where he spent his days in museums, the 1930 letter stating his aim to paint Brazilian life, Evicted 1934, Carnegie 1935, MoMA 1940, Library of Congress murals 1942, Paris show 1946, War and Peace panels 14 by 10 metres, Burial in a Hammock at Brussels 1958). Holder-curated and favourable; its political entries are not used.

Projeto Portinari, 'Critic Reviews', Google Arts & Culture story, read in full: quotations from French and Latin American critics, historians and writers praising his work (René Huyghe, Germain Bazin, Jean Cassou and others), with Bazin noting that the unmeasured violence of the expressionist works might shock Paris. Curated by the artist's archive, so almost entirely praise; used only as evidence of how critics responded, not for behaviour.

Israel Pedrosa, 'O Pintor do Novo Mundo' (essay delivered at the 2009 colloquium 'Portinari in Paris: 1946-2009', hosted on the Projeto Portinari site), read in full: a laudatory interpretation of his realism, the 1946 Charpentier show in Paris with a preface by Germain Bazin, and a description of the War and Peace panels (commissioned in 1952 through Itamaraty, delivered in January 1956, installed at the United Nations in September 1957), noting that he made preliminary models for the large panels. The author is affiliated with the Portinari Project; partisan.

Library of Congress, International Collections blog, 'If These Walls Could Talk: A Virtual Tour of the Hispanic Division's Candido Portinari Murals' (2 April 2021), read in full: Librarian of Congress Archibald MacLeish invited him to paint four murals for the Hispanic Reading Room, completed in 1941, under a joint commission of the Brazilian and United States governments in the context of the Good Neighbor Policy. Gives no detail of his method.

Jessica Sequeira, 'Portinari', Brasil Wire, read in full: a sympathetic but critical essay saying early Brazilian critics called his work demoralising and 'big foot' painting, that critics at home reassessed him favourably after honours abroad such as the Carnegie recognition, that his figures grew to fill the canvas with exaggerated heads, hands and feet, that he moved to thick brushwork and palette knife in the 1940s, and arguing that his nationalism served the elite art world more than the people he painted. COUNTER-VOICE.

persistence.rationale: [src_portinari_moma1940, src_portinari_brasilwire, src_portinari_gac_career | 1920s-1930s | museum catalogue + critical press + archive] The 1940 MoMA catalogue says his professors saw 'a stubborn persistence' in him, that for ten years he kept painting pictures of Brazilian life that no one wanted to buy (most piled up unsold) while portraits paid the rent, and that his painting of Brazilian life met open disapproval in Rio; Brasil Wire records early critics calling it demoralising; the archive's chronology shows the work continuing to the Carnegie recognition in 1935 and beyond. Documented across contemporary and later sources.

independent_thinking.rationale: [src_portinari_moma1940, src_portinari_brasilwire | 1930s | museum catalogue + critical press] The catalogue profile says he painted Brazil's Black and mulatto people although Brazilians objected, and that he ignored explicit hints and instructions about what kind of people to paint in some commissions; Brasil Wire says early critics dismissed his work as 'big foot' painting. The independence is documented but the key claim is one admiring exhibition profile with no named commission. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 68 / 0.52 because the central claim rests on a single admiring contemporary profile that names no specific commission or exchange.

mastery_orientation.rationale: [src_portinari_moma1940, src_portinari_gac_career, src_portinari_usp | 1919-1939 | museum catalogue + archive + university] He trained at the National School of Fine Arts, drew painstakingly accurate portraits from small photographs for pay, spent the prize trip to Europe visiting galleries and reading and brought back almost no paintings (catalogue), and in Paris spent his days in museums, especially the Louvre, and studied at night (archive chronology). The 1939 Rio exhibition included many details and studies for the frescoes. A documented investment in study and craft; one source on the Paris routine is the artist's own archive.

planning_orientation.rationale: [src_portinari_moma1940, src_portinari_pedrosa, src_portinari_loc | 1938-1956 | museum catalogue + essay + library blog] The 1939 exhibition catalogue lists many studies and details for the Ministry of Education frescoes among its 269 items; Pedrosa says he made preliminary models for the large United Nations panels; the Library of Congress blog describes sketches and studies for its murals. Preparatory work for large commissions is documented, but no source narrates how he planned a particular work. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 66 / 0.52 because the process evidence is the existence of studies, with a partisan essay and a promotional blog as the descriptive sources and no account of an actual planning decision.

experimentation.rationale: [src_portinari_moma1940, src_portinari_brasilwire | 1930s-1940s | museum catalogue + critical press] Smith's catalogue essay describes concurrent, quite different handlings: solid portraits, simplified rhythmic frescoes, a looser gouache technique, and a series of small fantasy pictures, calling his art remarkably varied in technique, style and theme; Brasil Wire adds that his figures grew to fill the canvas and that he moved to thick brushwork and palette knife in the 1940s. Documented stylistic variety, but largely a curator's description of results and not of his working process.
